content: To effectively implement rubella vaccination for women of reproductive age (WRA), collaboration with midwives, trained delivery attendants, maternity nurses, and partners is essential. All individuals involved in patient care, including healthcare professionals, residents, students, laboratory staff, and public health workers such as field workers, epidemiologists, and community health workers, must be engaged in this effort. The introduction of the rubella vaccine into national immunization programs, as well as programs aligned with the Every Newborn Action Plan, provides an opportunity to enhance the coverage of other critical vaccines, such as the birth dose of Hepatitis B, oral polio vaccine (OPV), and Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for infants. The rubella vaccine should be administered as part of the Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine, alongside the first dose of a measles-containing vaccine (MCV1). The age for administering MCV1 depends on the country’s immunization schedule. All unvaccinated older children, regardless of age, should be offered the MR vaccine whenever they come into contact with health services. This includes recording doses given to children older than 12 months. Since the MR vaccine replaces the measles-only vaccine, there are minimal programmatic implications in terms of procurement, storage, distribution, and use at the service delivery level. The training required for health workers to implement childhood rubella vaccination is minimal, focusing primarily on the transition to a combination vaccine that includes rubella and the associated key communication messages. Storage requirements, transport methods, and precautions for the MR vaccine are identical to those for the measles-only vaccine. Unlike the measles vaccine, which has lower seroconversion rates when administered before 12 months of age (necessitating two doses), the rubella vaccine achieves seroconversion in over 95% of children after a single dose, even at 9 months of age. Because rubella is less infectious than measles, it can be eliminated with a single dose of the rubella-containing vaccine (RCV) if high coverage is achieved. To simplify supply chain management and avoid complications, countries implementing a routine two-dose schedule for measles vaccination are advised to use the same combined MR vaccine for both doses. The estimated target population for MR vaccination is the same as that for MCV1 (and MCV2 in a two-dose schedule). The only change is the form of the vaccine, switching from monovalent measles to MR or MMR. For the first dose, the target population includes children surviving until 12 months of age. For the second dose, the target population includes children surviving until 15–18 months of age. If MCV2 is administered at school entry (5–6 years of age), the target population includes children surviving until 5 years of age. In practice, estimating population sizes by single year of age can be challenging, so the number of live births is often used as a proxy for annual cohorts under 5 years of age. The plan for introducing RCV should be integrated with the measles elimination plan, as the diseases have similar clinical presentations in children, and the rubella vaccine is administered as a combined MR vaccine. Countries preparing to introduce RCV must update their comprehensive multi-year plan (cMYP) and develop a specific plan of action for rubella control/elimination and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) prevention/elimination. This plan should include epidemiological data, vaccination strategies, surveillance activities, cold chain capacity, communication strategies, monitoring and evaluation, and budget and financing. High RCV coverage must be maintained through routine immunization or supplementary immunization activities (SIAs), with additional efforts to vaccinate WRA and health workers. The introduction of RCV by replacing the monovalent measles vaccine with MR is less complex than adding a standalone new vaccine. However, it is still beneficial to refer to WHO guidelines for adding a new vaccine to a national immunization program. These guidelines provide checklists and tools for planning and implementation. The cost of introducing RCV extends beyond the increase in vaccine costs. Immunization program budgets and financing plans must be updated using tools such as WHO’s “Immunization Costing and Financing” guide. This tool helps estimate costs, financing needs, and funding gaps to achieve coverage goals (>95% for rubella, as it is combined with measles vaccine). Countries eligible for Gavi support must prepare and update a cMYP when applying for funding. All countries, regardless of Gavi eligibility, benefit from detailed budgeting. Effective communication strategies, social mobilization, and training of health workers at all levels are critical for the successful introduction of RCV. Expanding cold chain and storage capacities, strengthening vaccine transport systems, and revising child health/vaccination cards and related materials are also necessary. In the short term, changes to materials can be made manually until stocks are depleted and reprinted. Opportunities for integrating MR delivery with other health services include combining the MR second dose with a DTP booster, distributing long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) for malaria control, or administering MR with the third dose of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV3) at 9–15 months of age. MR vaccination can also be provided to WRA during premarital counseling, HIV/AIDS screening, or postpartum care. School-based vaccination programs can integrate MR with HPV vaccination for girls or Td/TT immunizations, potentially including other adolescent health services or education. Collaboration with the Ministry of Education and school teachers is essential for school-based interventions. Rubella vaccine presentations include MR, MMR, and monovalent rubella vaccines (not available through UNICEF). MR vaccine procured through UNICEF comes in 10-dose vials, with the same volume as 10-dose measles vaccine vials. The vaccine is freeze-dried and requires reconstitution with a specific diluent provided by the manufacturer. The number of doses required for MR vaccine introduction remains the same as for measles vaccine. If a routine two-dose schedule is introduced, vaccine requirements will double if coverage for the second dose matches the first. High wastage rates (45–60%) are common with measles and MR vaccines due to multi-dose vial policies, which require discarding vials at the end of an immunization session or within six hours of opening. Introducing a two-dose schedule may reduce wastage rates by up to 40%, as some doses will be used for MCV2. Vaccinating non-pregnant mothers and health workers can also reduce wastage. Vaccine wastage should be monitored at all levels, and data should inform future supply forecasting, including diluent and injection supplies. Switching from a one-dose to a two-dose schedule for MR vaccination may reduce current measles vaccine wastage rates. Monitoring wastage and using data for forecasting is essential to optimize vaccine supply and reduce waste.
